concept_note: Moved earlier than first pass (ENIAC 1945) to Colossus (Dec 1943 / Feb 1944) because Colossus was a working programmable electronic machine; fit is partial since it was not stored-program. No mass_adoption: mainframes were not used routinely by ordinary people (UNIVAC's 1952 election night raised awareness only).

First pass (1931 MIT differential analyzer) was too late if tide-predicting machines count (1873); low confidence because they sum harmonics rather than solve general equations. Mass adoption none: analog computers served specialists.
Added the Baltimore-era trial (1886, vs 1887 elsewhere) as demonstration and kept 1890 census as practical use. No mass_adoption: business and government equipment, not used by ordinary people.

Moved much earlier than the first pass (1952 NC): pinned-barrel and perforated-roll machines (c. 850; 1725) fit the definition. Both low. No mass_adoption: Jacquard looms and NC were industrial tools.
Demonstration confirmed (Kilby 1958); added practical use 1961 (low). No mass_adoption milestone: ICs became ubiquitous in products, but no sourced year.

First pass had none; Wikipedia says GE built a cryotron demonstration computer after 1957, year approximate. No practical use (cryotron work abandoned; no commercial superconducting computer as of 2016) and no mass adoption.
Moved to 1898 (Poulsen) and 1903 commercial Telegraphone from RAMAC 1956. No mass_adoption year found (home tape recorders in early 1950s).
Kept Dancer 1839 as low-confidence demonstration; practical use moved from 1928 Recordak to 1870 Dagron pigeon-post microfilm. No mass_adoption sourced.

Moved earlier to Shepard Gismo/IMRC 1952 (low); kept 1965 USPS as practical use (low); no mass adoption.
Creeper 1971 as demonstration and Morris 1988 as practical use (mapping loose); earlier insider fraud and phone hacking noted; no mass adoption.

Moved the first demonstration from Starfish Prime (1962) back to Trinity (1945), where recording equipment was paralyzed despite shielding; Starfish Prime is the first damage to civilian electronics. No practical-use or mass-adoption milestone: it is a hazard, and hardening has no distinct sourced first event.

Kept Audrey (1952) as demonstration, rejected Radio Rex (1922) as a sound-triggered switch. Added a practical-use date (1984, low; probably earlier) and corrected the Siri date to 14 Oct 2011 (the first pass date was the announcement). Voice-operated doors not found.

First pass had only NaturallySpeaking 1997, which was a continuous-speech product, not the first. Added IBM Tangora (mid-1980s, low) and DragonDictate 1990; the 1956 RCA phonetic typewriter is probably the real first but could not be sourced. No mass-adoption milestone sourced.

First pass named the 1939 Voder; the earlier Kempelen speaking machine (1791 description) fits the definition and is earlier but weakly dated. Added practical use (1976, low) and mass adoption (Siri 2011, low). Kratzenstein 1779 rejected as vowels only.
Kept ELIZA (1966) with the year only; added ChatGPT as mass adoption (Nov 2022). No first_practical_use found.

Kept Georgetown-IBM (7 Jan 1954), noting the same-year Birkbeck APEXC demonstration. Practical use stays 1959 (low) with a conflicting 1964 Mark II date reported; added Babel Fish 1997 as mass adoption (low).
No milestones. No machine has decoded an unknown language from samples from samples, so there is no demonstration to date.

First pass named Colossus (1944); the Polish bomba (1938) is earlier and breaks Enigma by testing settings, so it replaces it as the demonstration. Cyclometer (c. 1934-35) noted as a catalogue aid. Practical use same date, low. No mass_adoption: not applicable.

First pass had Strachey 1953; found John Clark's Eureka (1845) as an earlier mechanical verse generator, and Strachey is dated summer 1952 by the sources, so the computer-only date is 1952. Added FoG weather forecasts (early 1990s) as practical use and ChatGPT (2022) as mass adoption.

Moved the demonstration from Illiac Suite (1957) to CSIRAC playing music (1950); the Illiac Suite remains the first composition by computer. AARON and other computer art noted but not made milestones. No practical-use or mass-adoption milestone sourced.

Replaced Samuel's 1959 paper with SNARC (1951, low) as the earliest clear learning machine; Theseus (1950), Homeostat (1948), Samuel (1952/1959) and the perceptron considered. No practical-use or mass-adoption milestone sourced.

Demonstration set to 1957 (first full chess games), with Los Alamos 1956 a variant and Turing/Prinz earlier but not playing games on a machine. Added practical use: Chess Challenger, March 1977. No mass-adoption date sourced.
Replaced Strachey's 1951-52 draughts with the Nimatron (1940), a machine that played Nim against the public. Demonstration and practical use are one event. No mass adoption.
No milestones: no machine matches human intelligence across all intellectual tasks, so there is no demonstration to date.

No milestone. The JPL STAR (Self-Testing And Repairing) computer, breadboard running a program in March 1969 (search snippet), is the likely first demonstration, but I could not fetch a page to quote, so it is dropped. SAPO (1951) used voting to mask faults but did not repair itself.
